title: The research shelf
intro: Published research on civic participation and public-budget transparency. Where findings are mixed, both sides are listed.

themes.claim: 1 — History of direct participation in American local government
themes.summary: New England towns have governed by open assembly since the 1630s. Tocqueville, in Democracy in America (vol. 1), wrote that “Town-meetings are to liberty what primary schools are to science.”

citations.label: Town meeting — four centuries of practice
Britannica — direct democracy: history and forms
Tocqueville — Democracy in America, vol. 1 (Project Gutenberg)

themes.claim: 2 — Trust in government and civic connection
themes.summary: Pew Research (2019) found three-quarters of Americans say trust in the federal government is shrinking. Putnam’s Bowling Alone documents two generations of decline in civic connection, from meeting attendance to league bowling.

citations.label: Pew Research — Americans' declining trust in government and each other (2019)
Pew Research — trust and distrust in America (full report)

themes.summary: Studies on transparency and trust: some find open budgeting and clear communication raise trust; others find disclosure without a government response lowers engagement (Crepaz 2024; Schnell 2023).

citations.label: Crepaz (2024) — transparency regulation, political trust, perceived corruption (survey experiment)

themes.claim: 4 — Effects of deliberation and participatory budgeting on participants
themes.summary: A structured deliberation study reported knowledge gains and higher civic engagement and voting nearly a year later (Stanford FSI; APSR). People Powered, an organization that promotes participatory budgeting, reports that participatory budgeting raised political activity and turnout among groups that usually vote less.

citations.label: Stanford FSI — the lasting effects of deliberation on civic engagement

themes.summary: Polis is a tool that clusters participants’ votes on short statements. In Taiwan, vTaiwan processes produced regulation recommendations (Participedia).

themes.claim: 6 — Participation platforms and processes used by governments
themes.summary: Switzerland votes about 15 times a year at the local level (Direct Democracy at the Local Level in Switzerland). Better Reykjavik is run by the Citizens Foundation (Citizens Foundation). Madrid’s Decide Madrid platform put residents’ top proposals into the draft budget (Participedia). Barcelona’s open-source Decidim platform runs many instances (Barcelona City Council). The UK Parliament responds to petitions that reach 10,000 signatures (UK Parliament petitions). Vermont’s Front Porch Forum: 81% of members reported feeling more informed, versus 26% on Facebook (Center for Media Engagement; Seven Days).

themes.summary: Sources describe problems with binding, high-volume ballot measures in California and Porto Alegre’s reliance on political champions to sustain participatory budgeting. Some research finds fears that voters are incompetent or easily captured are largely overstated.

themes.claim: 8 — Public choice theory and year-end spending
themes.summary: Public choice economics (James Buchanan won the 1986 Nobel in economics for this work) studies officials as people responding to the incentives they face. Niskanen’s 1971 model describes an agency that maximizes its budget; Wildavsky described incrementalism, in which next year’s budget builds on this year’s base. Liebman & Mahoney (AER 2017) found federal spending in the last week of the fiscal year is 4.9 times the weekly average, and that year-end projects were rated lower in quality.

themes.summary: Elinor Ostrom shared the 2009 Nobel in economics. Her field research found communities can govern commons durably when the governed help make the rules, monitoring is answerable to the community, and conflict resolution is cheap.

citations.label: Ostrom — Governing the Commons (Cambridge)
